II-H-01.note: Key B unique: A invents a chronology ('postdate') the text never gives, C's 'abandoned' contradicts the contemporaneous contrast, D reverses which structure held most grain. B and C share a first clause, which is the only real work; among the two, C overclaims. Template member 1 of 6 (concessive pivot). Answerable blind by picking the balanced two-clause option.

II-H-02.note: Key D unique. A flatly contradicts the opening (colonial vocabulary 'dominates the lexicon of commerce'), B is the exact reversal of the passage's thesis, C is an out-of-scope data-quality doubt. All three fail on a single word; no option competes with D.

II-H-03.note: Key A unique. C (mating success) and D (learning from neighbors vs parents) are off-topic subjects the passage never raises, so the item is really a 2-way choice between A and B, and B ('overstated by earlier studies') attacks data the text presents as sound. Two dead options makes this the weakest distractor set in 01-06.

II-H-04.note: Key C unique. A is a decent trap (swaps what the pigment/ring evidence can show: it dates, it identifies no hand), B overgeneralizes to 'art historians generally', D reverses the ring-count direction ('postdates' vs inside the final decade). The stage-splitting key is well made.

II-H-05.note: Key D unique. C is the arithmetic-inversion trap (has the daily rate falling when the text says 'rising steadily') and is the only distractor that requires reading; A adds a population (weavers elsewhere) the ledgers do not cover, B imports a source-reliability suspicion the text never raises.

II-H-06.note: Key B unique: it is the only option reporting both halves of the result (time explains most; a concrete-word residual survives). A supplies an untested mechanism, C inverts which word type carried the residual, D relabels the slow-reading explanation as a scoring artifact.

II-H-07.note: FLAGGED PAIR ADJUDICATED - key A stands, D is not defensible. The proposal's distinctive claim is frequency ('seeing use only rarely'); A is the ONLY option carrying any evidence about amount of use. D ('polish produced by contact with wood') establishes that batons touched shafts, which the first camp already asserts from 'the polished interior of each baton's bored hole' - it supports the pure-tool hypothesis at least as strongly as the middle position, so it cannot be what 'most strongly' supports the researcher over that rival. AUTHORING BLEMISH, not a key error: A's clause 'while plainer batons show substantially heavier wear' does cut against 'circulated mainly as marks of standing' for the class as a whole, which is what made blind solvers wobble. Recommend editing A to scope the plain batons as a minority (e.g. 'while the plainer minority show heavier wear') before insert.

II-H-08.note: Key C unique - an exclusion experiment in the warmest part of the region separates the two accounts, which is what the stem asks. A supports the account being argued against, B makes warming an upstream cause of the urchin outbreak and so ties the accounts together rather than separating them, D looks pro-urchin until the passage supplies 'thinned at similar rates whether... southern... or... northern'. D is the reason the passage does real work here.

II-H-09.note: Key B unique: handwriting places identifiable non-borrowers inside the volumes, which is the external evidence the critics demand. A counts only registered borrowings, C narrows the circle the historian wants to widen, D (late returns) is the one genuine trap since it is equally consistent with one slow reader.

II-H-10.note: FLAGGED PAIR ADJUDICATED - key D stands, B is not defensible. B (carrying stilted ants part-way) is a real result but follows from ANY walked-distance odometer, optic-flow integration included, so it discriminates nothing and fails the stem's 'over the alternatives'. D is the only option that holds a rival variable still. STEM IMPRECISION, worth fixing: the skeptics name three alternatives (gait, speed, optic flow) and D neutralizes only the visual one, so 'the alternatives the skeptics raise' overpromises. Recommend narrowing the stem to the visual alternative, or adding a clause to D that also fixes walking speed; the key does not change either way.

II-H-11.note: CONFIRMS the blind solvers. A is direct documentary evidence naming a person; B (sales figures) and D (women published anonymously, i.e. mere possibility) are not about this pamphlet at all, and C intensifies the very inference the objection already defeated. Easiest item in 07-12 and answerable from the options alone.

II-H-12.note: CONFIRMS the blind solvers on difficulty and distractors, and I would add passage_needed=false: C is the only option naming a volcanic source, and A, B and D all visibly favor the colleague rather than the geologist. A solver needs neither the passage nor the objection.

II-H-13.note: Key D verified against the figures: transpiration 620/505/390/300 falls monotonically, yield 4.1/4.4/4.0/3.1 peaks at 20 percent. A is false twice, C is false (transpiration peaks unshaded), B's second half is false (3.1 < 4.1). All three distractors die on arithmetic rather than on reasoning. NEAR-DUPLICATE of II-H-17 - see that note.

II-H-14.note: Key B verified: 11.4 x 0.58 = 6.61, 6.9 x 0.96 = 6.62. Best quantitative item in the batch because A and C are both TRUE statements that simply do not bear on post-sorting recovery, and D is a near miss (0.42 x 11.4 = 4.79, not 'about as much as' 6.9). Distractors that are true-but-irrelevant are what the other quantitative items lack.

II-H-15.note: Key C verified: site 3 has 38 burrows vs site 2's 22 with 9 cm vs 11 cm of retreat. A is false at site 3 (9 cm, not >10), D is false (11+9=20 of 50 cm, i.e. 40 percent), and B is true but argues FOR the relationship the researcher questions - the strongest distractor here. Minor: 38/22 = 1.73 is a stretch for 'nearly twice', though no other option survives. The gravel-bar sentence is an unused red herring, which is fine.

II-H-16.note: Key A verified (3 of 12 schools = a quarter). B is false (1 vs 9 is about a ninth, not 'less than a tenth'), C is false and inverted (A spans 1-11, B spans 9-10.4), D is false (A's 11 exceeds all of B's). Sound but every distractor is a false statement, so it rewards checking rather than reasoning.

II-H-17.note: Key B verified: nitrogen 34/51/66/74 monotone, worms 62/78/71/39 rising then dropping below the unamended 62. C is false (maxima at different rates), D half-false (74 vs 66 is not 'roughly double'), and A is TRUE but shows the two measures moving together, which is the good distractor. STRUCTURAL DUPLICATE of II-H-13 - see the template adjudication; one of the two should be re-authored, not both inserted. DROPPED: functionally identical to II-H-13 (same key sentence shape, monotone vs inverted-U series); solving one gives the other. Keeping 13.

II-H-18.note: Key D verified: novices 1.9->2.6 s and 33->41 percent (0.7 s, 8 points); experienced 1.2->1.3 s and 57->58 percent (0.1 s, 1 point). B is false (8 > 1), C is false (0.7 vs 0.1 is the whole point), A is true but compares absolute levels rather than the change. Solvers grouped this with 13 and 17; it is a 2x2 group design with a paired-delta key, a genuinely different shape.

II-H-19.note: Key C unique. B overreads 'rudimentary but light-responsive' into vision loss being 'reversed within a single generation', D overshoots from 'not this kind of selection' to 'no selection at all', A asserts a chronology the text never supplies. The chromosomal-adjacency detail makes the hitchhiking reading the only one the evidence licenses.

II-H-20.note: CONFIRMS the blind solvers on both counts. Three simultaneous changes plus a 'would be justified in concluding' stem telegraph a confounding answer, and A is the only option of that kind. B ranks effects with no basis, C reverses the direction (better-known reporting would RAISE reported illness), D proposes a future study instead of concluding. Easiest item in the batch.

II-H-21.note: Key D unique and this is the item where the passage does the most work. C ('a systematic error of about forty minutes introduced in the course of copying') is genuinely attractive and is defeated ONLY by the passage's statement that the tide arrives progressively later moving south - a scribal slip does not predict a shift matching the physical gradient. A contradicts 'nothing in either copy indicates that its scribe had seen the other's'; B is out of scope. Best-constructed item in the batch.

II-H-22.note: Key B unique. A is the real trap: it presupposes warehouse age accounted for the whole effect, which is the very thing the restricted comparison exists to test. C misstates what the sample was matched on (warehouse age and record detail, not efficiency), D asserts a selective removal the matching does not perform.

II-H-23.note: Key A unique. Same pigment, same wall, two outcomes, so the pigment cannot be the variable. B is self-defeating (lower portico UV would protect the plaster passages too), C attaches the conclusion to moisture, never mentioned, D states the observed pattern backward - the pigment faded precisely where it sat on plaster.

II-H-24.note: Key C unique. D is the strong distractor and needs the passage to kill: excluding trunks and limbs still leaves the sub-30 cm soil where 'the comparison reverses', so the figure would not hold even then. A adds a decay fact not in the text and points the wrong way, B trades one partial measure for another. The 'chosen because cores are most easily taken' detail is what makes the bounded-claim reading correct rather than merely available.
